Title: Decoding the Project Gutenberg license: what you can and must do with a public‑domain eBook
Description: Use the Gettysburg Address eBook as a concrete example to explain the Project Gutenberg License’s core permissions and obligations: what distributors and users are allowed to do with public‑domain texts (copy, modify, redistribute, create derivatives) and which mandatory conditions accompany that freedom (retain the full license, display a required notice, format and distribution rules, refund/replacement rights).
Audience: Librarians, educators, digital archivists, open‑content distributors, and developers who handle public‑domain texts
Rationale: Many readers assume 'public domain' means free of all constraints. The source demonstrates that Project Gutenberg combines broad reuse rights with specific legal and operational requirements. Explaining those obligations clearly (with exact clauses) prevents accidental noncompliance and helps organizations reuse texts correctly.
Evidence: Explicit statements in the eBook header and license: “This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere ... You may copy it, give it away or re‑use it under the terms of the Project Gutenberg License” (front matter). License clauses require prominent display of a specific notice whenever a Project Gutenberg work is distributed (1.E.1), forbid removing the full Project Gutenberg License (1.E.4), require including the license with redistributed works (1.E.5), and describe limited warranty/replacement rights (1.F.3–1.F.4). The work also notes practical format rules (1.E.6) and distribution limitations (1.E.7).
